subject: english-literature
title: Intertextual Echoes
welcome_lead: No text exists in isolation. Kristeva's intertextuality reminds us that every work is a tissue of citations, allusions, and dialogues with what came before.
meta_desc: English Literature: intertextuality, allusion, and the dialogic nature of texts.
final_note: Every text is a conversation — listen for who else is speaking.

concepts.def: Julia Kristeva's concept that texts derive meaning through relationships with other texts.
A brief, often indirect reference to another text, event or figure.
Bakhtin's notion that texts contain multiple voices in dialogue.
An earlier text upon which a later text (hypertext) is built (Genette).
A text written over an earlier one, where traces of the original remain visible.
An imitation of another work's style, often as homage rather than mockery.

walkthroughs.body_html: T S Eliot's The Waste Land alludes to Dante, Shakespeare, and the Upanishads. Identifying the source enriches meaning: the allusion imports the earlier context.
For Bakhtin, the novel is fundamentally polyphonic — many voices contend within it. Dostoevsky's characters speak with ideological independence, not as mouthpieces for the author.
Genette calls the source text the hypotext and the derivative the hypertext. Joyce's Ulysses is a hypertext of Homer's Odyssey — knowing the structure unlocks the parallels.

mcqs.q: What is the dramatic function of a soliloquy?
options: A soliloquy is any long speech a character gives.
A soliloquy is when characters argue with each other.
The narrator and author are different words for the same thing.
It reveals a character's inner thoughts directly to the audience while the character is alone on stage — a convention granting access to private psychology.

mcqs.q: Why must students distinguish the narrator from the author?
options: The narrator is a constructed voice within the text; the author is the real person who created it. Conflating them misreads irony, unreliable narration and persona.
The narrator and author are different words for the same thing.
The narrator's views are always the author's views.
A soliloquy is when characters argue with each other.
When the audience knows something a character does not, creating tension between the character's words/actions and the audience's understanding.
Dramatic irony is when something ironic happens in a play.
A soliloquy is when characters argue with each other.
Dramatic irony is when characters speak in dramatic voices.
